description: We are a two-person team of 12-year-old students from Iran, passionate about programming, space, and climate science. We are working on a project called AI Climate Guardian, which uses NASA climate data to study warming trends across different regions of Iran. Our team is complete.
summary: We built AI Climate Guardian, a data analysis tool that uses NASA POWER temperature data (from the MERRA-2 model) to compare July temperature trends from 2019 to 2026 in four US climate zones: Phoenix, Seattle, Denver and Miami. It answers the challenge by showing what is changing (July air temperature), where (four climates) and how much (degrees C per year). Denver warmed fastest and Seattle showed an unexpected cooling trend, which we treat as a clue, not proof, because we used only 8 years of data.
details: Question: Is the July temperature trend the same across different US climate zones, or are some regions changing faster, or even in the opposite direction? Data: NASA POWER, parameter T2M (air temperature at 2 m) from the MERRA-2 reanalysis model, not a direct satellite sensor reading; about 0.5 degree resolution, daily. Cities: Phoenix (hot desert), Seattle (temperate oceanic), Denver (cold semi-arid highland), Miami (humid subtropical).Method: for each city we averaged the daily temperature of July for each year from 2019 to 2026 and fitted a least-squares line to get the trend in degrees Celsius per year. Data cleaning: our first averages looked clearly wrong (a negative temperature), so with Claude's help we traced the cause to NASA POWER's -999 missing-value marker and removed all values below -900 before calculating.Results (degrees C per year): Denver +0.185, Miami +0.113, Phoenix +0.051, Seattle -0.256. Denver warmed fastest. Seattle was the surprise: it shows a cooling trend. July trends are not the same across regions, and not always in the same direction.Limitations: only 8 years, one month per year, one dataset. Seattle's cooling is driven mostly by two unusually cool Julys (2025 and 2026), and Denver's warming is helped by a warm July 2026, so we treat these as clues, not proof. We do not claim statistical significance with only 8 points. T2M is a model product, and our slope is a simple indicator.Use of AI: we used Claude (Anthropic), a large language model chatbot. Claude helped design the analysis, wrote the Python code and drafted the demo slides. Our team chose the four US cities, ran and tested the code, noticed the wrong averages, and interpreted the results. The charts were produced by this code from NASA data. No images, video or audio were generated by AI.
